title: Validation, HTTP errors, and status codes

spans.text: WHY USE THIS?
FastAPI builds JSON APIs that web and mobile applications call over HTTP; type annotations help validate inputs and describe the API contract.
PURPOSE AND REAL-WORLD USE

An API should respond clearly to both accepted and rejected requests. FastAPI returns 422 for request validation failures; `HTTPException` represents application decisions such as a missing resource (404). `status_code` describes the successful response.

To run these examples locally, install `pip install fastapi uvicorn httpx` plus any extra package named in the lesson. Save the server example as `app.py` and start `uvicorn app:app --reload`. `--reload` is for development only.

WHERE DOES THIS APPEAR IN REAL LIFE?
A shop returns 404 for a missing item and 201 after successfully creating one.
If this part is omitted: Without an explicit error and suitable status, clients cannot distinguish failure from success or choose a recovery action.

spans.text:
LINE-BY-LINE CODE EXPLANATION
`from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, status` — Imports a required type or tool; without it, the name is unavailable.
`app = FastAPI()` — `FastAPI()` creates the ASGI application that holds the routes and is passed to the server.
`items = {1: {"name": "pen"}}` — Continues the application's data handling or control flow.
`@app.get("/items/{item_id}", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)` — Binds an HTTP method and URL path to this function; without the decorator, it is not an API endpoint.
`async def read_item(item_id: int):` — Defines the endpoint the server calls; parameter names help bind path, query, or body data.
`item = items.get(item_id)` — Runs work for this request; its result or side effect affects the response.
`if item is None:` — Chooses a branch when the condition is true and handles an edge case.
`raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")` — Stops the request with an explicit status and error detail instead of hiding the failure.
`return item` — Returns the HTTP response value; FastAPI converts it to JSON and applies the response model.
PRACTICE: CHECK IT WITH AN HTTP CLIENT
This complete file calls the app locally with TestClient; it does not open a server port. Install `httpx` for TestClient.
COMPLETE RUNNABLE CLIENT TEST
QUESTION: What will this code print? Predict first, then run it.

spans.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, status

app = FastAPI()
items = {1: {"name": "pen"}}

@app.get("/items/{item_id}", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    item = items.get(item_id)
    if item is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return item

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

with TestClient(app) as client:
    response = client.get("/items/99")
    print(response.status_code, response.json())

spans.text: EXPECTED CLIENT-TEST OUTPUT

LINE-BY-LINE CODE EXPLANATION
`from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, status` — Imports a required type or tool; without it, the name is unavailable.
`app = FastAPI()` — `FastAPI()` creates the ASGI application that holds the routes and is passed to the server.
`items = {1: {"name": "pen"}}` — Continues the application's data handling or control flow.
`@app.get("/items/{item_id}", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)` — Binds an HTTP method and URL path to this function; without the decorator, it is not an API endpoint.
`async def read_item(item_id: int):` — Defines the endpoint the server calls; parameter names help bind path, query, or body data.
`item = items.get(item_id)` — Runs work for this request; its result or side effect affects the response.
`if item is None:` — Chooses a branch when the condition is true and handles an edge case.
`raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")` — Stops the request with an explicit status and error detail instead of hiding the failure.
`return item` — Returns the HTTP response value; FastAPI converts it to JSON and applies the response model.
`from fastapi.testclient import TestClient` — Imports TestClient so an HTTP request can exercise the app without opening a server port.
`with TestClient(app) as client:` — Creates a test HTTP client for the app and closes it when the context ends.
`response = client.get("/items/99")` — Sends the stated GET request through the test client and stores the response.
`print(response.status_code, response.json())` — Reads and prints both the HTTP status code and parsed JSON response.
COMMON MISTAKES
Returning 200 for every outcome or exposing internal tracebacks; choose an appropriate status and keep internals out of responses.

spans.title: Practical tip
spans.text: For a successful POST that creates a resource, use `status_code=201`; test both success and missing-resource cases.

spans.title: One level deeper
spans.text: 422 indicates request-shape/type validation failure; 404 means the application could not find a resource. Test them separately.

spans.title: Important warning
spans.text: Do not use `assert` for user input: optimized Python can remove assertions. Use validation and `HTTPException` for API errors.
QUICK RECALL
Question: Which action best prevents the common mistake from this lesson?
Answer: For a successful POST that creates a resource, use `status_code=201`; test both success and missing-resource cases.
